Issued at 315 AM EST Tue Nov 10 2026

Early this morning GOES water vapor imagery and GFS 500mb model 
height analysis showed an upper level low pressure over Newfoundland 
and Labrador with west-northwest flow over the Great Lakes region. 
Shortwaves could be seen embedded in the flow with one passing north 
of Lake Superior. IR imagery showed passing high clouds over the 
southern U.P. but otherwise is was clear over the north and east. 
Despite the clear skies temperatures had stayed warmer in the wake 
of a cold front due winds/mixing as isalobaric flow with pressure 
rises in the 2 to 3 mb per 6 hour range kept a breeze for most 
areas. Surface observations showed winds were gusting 25-30 mph over 
the Keweenaw and near Lake Superior. This was keeping temperatures 
in the 40s to low 50s with the exception of a few pockets of 30s 
over the interior, where the boundary layer had managed to decouple.

Another warm day for November is on tap for the U.P. with highs 
reaching the mid 40s north and mid 50s far south. This puts highs 
about 5-10 degrees above seasonal averages. This will be the last 
well above average day for a bit as cooler weather comes in for the 
later half of the week and into the weekend.

Tonight low pressure will track south of the area bringing 
increasing cloudiness to the area. An area of rain will accompany 
this low on the north side in an area of moderate fgen providing 
forcing coinciding with deeper moisture. Models diverge on the exact 
placement of this feature but felt confident enough to bring PoPs up 
over the southern half of the U.P. late tonight into Wednesday 
morning. NBM was running cold for tonight with temperatures below 
freezing over the interior. Given the increasing cloud cover and 
rain chances opted to blend in some raw (non-bias corrected) 
guidance.

Wednesday through Friday multiple shortwaves will drop south out of 
Canada as the upper low over Newfoundland shifts west, reaching Lake 
Huron by Friday. This will bring a sustained period of cold air 
advection to the area with 850mb temps falling into the -8 to -10C 
range, starting Wednesday afternoon. Thus expect temperatures to 
start out in the 40s for the first half of the day but we should see 
falling temperatures over the northern U.P. during the afternoon as 
a cold front pushes south and northerly flow develops. Widespread 
lake effect rain showers are expected to develop on Wednesday 
afternoon over the northern part of the U.P. as well. As 
temperatures cool through the evening expect snow to mix in over the 
higher terrain with a changeover to snow elsewhere as the night 
progresses. With continued caa and additional embedded shortwaves 
expect period of LES through Saturday morning with daytime 
temperatures (highs in the 30s) falling to near or slightly below 
average.

Several forecast challenges present themselves with this event and 
did quite a bit of deviation from the NBM (blended guidance) in the 
forecast package. NBM is struggling to handle the pattern change 
with daytime temperatures too warm and overnight lows too cold 
(trained on cool, clear nights). Warmed temperatures up quite a bit 
for Wednesday and Thursday night. NBM was indicating lows in the low 
to mid 20s over the interior with subfreezing temperatures to the 
Lake Superior shoreline. This seems unlikely given 850mb temps are 
only -8 to -10 and the lake temperatures are 8-10C. Additionally, 
widespread cloudiness and precipitation will limit cooling. Brought 
low up to around 34 near the lakeshore and low 30s over the eastern 
U.P., with upper 20s across the west for Wednesday night. Similar 
adjustments were made for Thursday night but might still be too cool 
given continued onshore flow and previously mentioned factors. As 
far as intensity and accumulations the NBM continues to struggle 
with QPF; blended in other guidance (REFS, Canadian) to bring up QPF 
amounts. Convergent flow favors at least a few more dominant bands 
setting up over the eastern half of Lake Superior with another band 
over the central part downwind of Lake Nipigon which should help 
prime the atmosphere (for moisture) and provide convergent flow in 
the low levels. Models have come into better agreement with the 
depth of moisture with most indicating at least some of the DGZ is 
intersected along with inversion heights up to 8kft (possibly higher 
over the relatively warm waters of Lake Superior). Thus moderate 
snowfall rates seem likely in the more dominant bands with the 
potential for brief heavy snow bursts over the higher terrain of the 
north-central and possibly Keweenaw. Marginally cold low levels and 
warm ground temperatures will probably keep snow ratios on the lower 
side but still expecting several inches of snowfall over the higher 
terrain (Keweenaw, Marquette County and Baraga County) Wednesday 
night through Friday, with the most impactful period being during
